summary: Registers the MIME type application/font-tdpfr for the Portable Font Resource format. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Fonts need a name tag so a computer knows what the file is. This registers the tag for one kind of font file.

questions: how do computers recognize pfr files
subtitle: Registers the MIME type for Portable Font Resource files.

tldr.problem: Portable Font Resource (PFR) files need an official MIME type so software can recognize and handle them correctly when transmitted over the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers the media type application/font-tdpfr with IANA, providing the official label and metadata that allows mail clients, web browsers, and other software to identify PFR font files.
tldr.outcome: The MIME type application/font-tdpfr is now standardized for PFR font files, making it possible for applications to reliably identify, accept, and process them.

today: RFC 3073 is informational and has not been obsoleted. The MIME type application/font-tdpfr is registered with IANA. While PFR fonts were adopted by some standards bodies, web and mail software more commonly use OpenType and TrueType formats, which are more widely standardized and supported.

sections.title: Why Register a MIME Type
sections.content:
When software receives a file over email or the web, it needs to know what kind of file it is in order to open it correctly. The MIME type (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) is the standard label that tells a computer what a file contains.

The Portable Font Resource (PFR) is a font format created by Bitstream Inc. Before this RFC, PFR files had an older, proprietary MIME type. This document registers the official, standardized MIME type application/font-tdpfr with IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority), making it the authoritative label for PFR files on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: When you get a file, your computer looks at the label to know what to do with it. This document creates an official label for PFR font files.

sections.title: What PFR Is
sections.content:
A PFR file is a compact, scalable font. It contains the shapes (glyphs) for the letters and symbols of a typeface, with each glyph linked to a character code. Because PFR glyphs are defined at high resolution independent of any specific output device, they can be displayed or printed at any size without loss of quality.

PFR is platform-independent (works on any operating system), supports optional bitmap images of glyphs alongside the scalable outlines, and is designed to be compact for efficient transmission. It was adopted as a standard font format by DAVIC (Digital Audio-Visual Council), DVB (Digital Video Broadcasting), and DTG (Digital Terrestrial Television Group), giving it industry backing beyond email.
sections.plainLanguage: PFR is a font file that can scale to any size without getting blurry and works on any computer.

sections.title: The MIME Type Registration
sections.content:
The registered media type is application/font-tdpfr. The registration specifies that PFR files are binary data (not text) and may need to be base64-encoded for safe transmission in email. The magic number (file signature) for PFR files is the four bytes 50 46 52 30 in hexadecimal, which is readable as "PFR0" in ASCII.

The file extension is .pfr, and the Macintosh creator code is 'b$pw' with the type 'PFR '. The IANA registration notes that PFR is intended for common (widespread) use and lists example applications that support it: Netscape Communicator, Bitstream WebFont Maker, and Hexmac Typograph.
sections.plainLanguage: The official name is application/font-tdpfr, and PFR files start with the bytes PFR0 so computers can spot them.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
PFR has an extensible structure that allows future enhancements. The RFC notes that the current PFR specification includes only descriptive fields (metadata) that do not trigger special behavior in receiving software, so the current format poses no additional security risks beyond those of rendering fonts in general.

However, the RFC acknowledges that future extensions to PFR could theoretically introduce fields that modify application behavior. The document emphasizes that any such capability would be inconsistent with the goals of the PFR specification and is not supported in the current version. The registration identifies no known interoperability issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Font files can be extended in the future, but the current PFR format is safe. Computers just read the glyph shapes; there is nothing that makes them do unexpected things.
